metadata.description: Comprehensive bee encyclopedia integrated from frontend data sources

Italian Honey Bee.characteristics: Lightly colored (light leather to yellow), long brood cycles, prone to robbing.
Italian Honey Bee.honey_yield: Very high (up to 150 lbs/hive in warm climates).
Italian Honey Bee.temperament: Extremely docile and gentle; ideal for beginners.
Italian Honey Bee.description: The most popular bee for commercial beekeeping worldwide due to its high productivity and gentle nature.

Carniolan Honey Bee.characteristics: Greyish-brown, thick hair; rapid spring buildup with ability to hibernate with small clusters.
Carniolan Honey Bee.temperament: Very gentle; excellent for suburban settings.
Carniolan Honey Bee.climate_suitability: Excellent cold tolerance; thrives in temperate to alpine zones.
cons: May swarm aggressively in strong nectar flows
Light-colored wax is less robust for comb foundation
Carniolan Honey Bee.description: Preferred by European beekeepers for its adaptability, gentle behavior, and resistance to diseases. Performs well in colder climates where forage windows are short.

Buckfast Bee.characteristics: Engineered for disease resistance; variable color from dark brown to yellow.
Buckfast Bee.temperament: Calm and easy to work; however, queen progeny can become more aggressive.
Buckfast Bee.climate_suitability: Very adaptable; thrives from Northern Europe to Africa.
cons: Genetic drift can produce aggressive colonies
Buckfast Bee.description: A legendary hybrid developed over decades by Brother Adam. Known for robust health and adaptability, it is the foundation of many modern breeding programs and a perfect match for BeeYield's precision apiary management.

African Honey Bee (Apis mellifera scutel.characteristics: Smaller body; extremely defensive; multiple mating flights for queens.
African Honey Bee (Apis mellifera scutel.temperament: Highly defensive ('Africanized' reputation); require experienced handling.
African Honey Bee (Apis mellifera scutel.climate_suitability: Thrives in tropical and arid climates; does not cluster well in cold.
cons: Very defensive behavior requires protective measures
African Honey Bee (Apis mellifera scutel.description: Native to the Kibwezi region and valued by BeeYield for genetic traits. Our colonies selectively breed scutellata with milder strains to combine disease resistance with manageable temperament.

Eastern Honey Bee (Apis cerana).characteristics: Smaller than western bees; dark coloring; colonies can consist of 6,000-8,000 bees.
Eastern Honey Bee (Apis cerana).climate_suitability: Tropical to subtropical; highly adapted to local diseases and predators.
Eastern Honey Bee (Apis cerana).description: Used in research for natural mite resistance behaviors, particularly hygienic grooming. BeeYield studies cerana behavior for integration into Scutellata breeding lines.

German Dark Bee.characteristics: Dark brown to black coloring; stocky body; adapted to long, cold winters.
German Dark Bee.temperament: Defensive under certain conditions; can be 'hot' during inspections.
German Dark Bee.climate_suitability: Superb cold hardiness; survives harsh Nordic winters.
cons: Can be defensive when colony is disturbed
German Dark Bee.description: The original European bee before Italian imports dominated. Now critically endangered in pure form but still found in conservation programs and mountain apiaries.

Caucasian Bee.characteristics: Long proboscis (7.2mm) for deep flowers; grey coloring; calm.
Caucasian Bee.temperament: Extremely gentle; heaviest propolis use of all subspecies.
Caucasian Bee.climate_suitability: Moderate cold tolerance; struggles with humid climates.
cons: Excessive propolizing makes hive management difficult
Caucasian Bee.description: Valued for unique flower access and pharmaceutical-grade propolis. BeeYield incorporates Caucasian genetics into targeted pollination contracts for deep-throated flowers like red clover.

Russian Bee.characteristics: Variable coloring; evolved alongside Varroa for 150+ years.
Russian Bee.temperament: Gentle but may rear queen cells liberally.
Russian Bee.climate_suitability: Cold-hardy; performs well in fluctuating spring temps.
cons: Multiple queen cells can confuse beginners
Russian Bee.description: Selected by USDA for mite-resistance breeding programs. BeeYield sources Russian queen genetics for natural IPM integration.

American Foulbrood (AFB).signs: Sunken, dark, perforated cappings; 'pupal tongue' protruding from remains.
American Foulbrood (AFB).symptoms: Larvae turn coffee-brown and ropy; distinct 'foul' decayed-fish odor. Scale adheres tightly to cell wall.
American Foulbrood (AFB).causes: Spore-forming bacteria ingested by young larvae. Spores remain viable for 40+ years.
American Foulbrood (AFB).detection: Rope Test (>2cm stretch); Holst Milk Test; EFD Diagnostic Kits.
American Foulbrood (AFB).treatment: Usage of antibiotics (Terramycin) only suppresses symptoms. Total incineration of hive, bees, and frames is the only reliable cure.
American Foulbrood (AFB).prevention: Regular inspection; tool sterilization; hygienic queens; avoiding buying used equipment without history.
American Foulbrood (AFB).transmission: Robbing; drifting; contaminated tools; swapping frames between hives.
American Foulbrood (AFB).myths: Freezing equipment kills spores (False); Honey from AFB hives is toxic to humans (False, but spreads disease to bees).

European Foulbrood (EFB).signs: Twisted, yellow/brown larvae coiled in 'C' shape; die before capping.
European Foulbrood (EFB).symptoms: Melted/rubbery larvae; sour/yeasty smell; spotty brood pattern. Tracheal system often visible.
European Foulbrood (EFB).causes: Bacterial infection exacerbated by nutritional stress or chilled brood.
European Foulbrood (EFB).treatment: Re-queening (break brood cycle); Shook Swarm method; antibiotic treatment (Oxytetracycline) where legal.
European Foulbrood (EFB).prevention: Maintain strong colonies; ensure adequate pollen/nectar flow; reduce stress.
European Foulbrood (EFB).transmission: Nurse bees feeding larvae; drifting; contaminated pollen.
European Foulbrood (EFB).myths: It always kills the colony (False, strong colonies can clear it); It smells like fish (False, smells sour).

Varroa Destructor.signs: Red-brown mites on adult bees; spotty brood pattern.
Varroa Destructor.symptoms: Parasitic Mite Syndrome (PMS); Deformed Wing Virus signs; rapid population crash in late summer.
Varroa Destructor.causes: Introduction of mites via drifting, robbing, or swarms.
Varroa Destructor.detection: Alcohol Wash (Threshold >3/100 bees); Sugar Roll; Sticky Board Drop.
Varroa Destructor.treatment: Organic Acids (Formic, Oxalic); Thymol (Apiguard); Synthetic Miticides (Amitraz, Flumethrin).
Varroa Destructor.prevention: VSH (Varroa Sensitive Hygiene) Queens; Drone Brood Removal; Screened Bottom Boards.
Varroa Destructor.myths: Freezing winter kills them (False); Natural bees don't need treatment (False, usually collapse).

Chalkbrood.signs: Hard, white/grey/black 'mummies' on bottom board or in cells.
Chalkbrood.symptoms: Spotty brood; audible 'rattle' when shaking frames of mummies.
Chalkbrood.causes: Fungal spores triggered by chilling, high humidity, or stress.
Chalkbrood.treatment: Self-limiting in strong hives. Re-queen if chronic. Increase ventilation. Feed syrup.
Chalkbrood.prevention: Place hives in full sun; avoid opening in cold weather; hygienic genetics.
Chalkbrood.myths: It kills the colony (Rarely, usually a stress indicator).

Stonebrood.signs: Larvae/pupae turn hard and stone-like; greenish fungal spores.
Stonebrood.symptoms: Mummified brood similar to Chalkbrood but harder; respiratory hazard for beekeeper.
Stonebrood.causes: Fungal infection often linked to damp conditions.
Stonebrood.treatment: Destruction of infected comb. Note: Zoonotic risk (can infect humans).
Stonebrood.myths: Harmless to humans (False, can cause Aspergillosis).

Nosema (Apis & Ceranae).signs: N. apis: Dysentery (fecal staining) on hive front. N. ceranae: No dysentery, simple dwindling.
Nosema (Apis & Ceranae).symptoms: Slow spring buildup; crawling bees; disjointed wings (K-wing); sudden population drop.
Nosema (Apis & Ceranae).causes: Spore ingestion; stress; poor nutrition; containment during winter.
Nosema (Apis & Ceranae).detection: Microscopy (hemocytometer count); Field gut squash (white gut = healthy, milky/swollen = infected).
Nosema (Apis & Ceranae).treatment: Fumagillin (where legal); Thymol supplements; probiotics; strong nutrition.
Nosema (Apis & Ceranae).prevention: Sunny apiary sites; good winter stores; crush-and-strain honey harvest (cycle combs).
Nosema (Apis & Ceranae).myths: Dysentery always means Nosema (False, can be dysentery from poor food).

Deformed Wing Virus (DWV).signs: Emerging bees with shriveled/crumpled wings; shortened abdomens.
Deformed Wing Virus (DWV).symptoms: Flightless bees crawling on ground; rapid colony collapse.
Deformed Wing Virus (DWV).causes: Vectored and amplified by Varroa destructor feeding on fat body.
Deformed Wing Virus (DWV).treatment: Treat the vector (Varroa). No direct antiviral cure available.

Acute Bee Paralysis Virus (ABPV).signs: Trembling; inability to fly; loss of hair (greasy look).
Acute Bee Paralysis Virus (ABPV).symptoms: Sudden death of large numbers of adult bees outside hive.

Chronic Bee Paralysis Virus (CBPV).signs: Type 1: Trembling wings/bodies ('Paralysis'). Type 2: 'Hairless black syndrome' (greasy, black bees).
Chronic Bee Paralysis Virus (CBPV).symptoms: Nibbling attacks by healthy bees on infected ones; piles of dead bees.
Chronic Bee Paralysis Virus (CBPV).myths: Old bees naturally turn black (True, but trembling is the key differentiator).

Sacbrood Virus (SBV).signs: Larvae die upright in cell; head turns dark/black ('Gondola shape'); fluid-filled 'sac'.
Sacbrood Virus (SBV).symptoms: Scales are brittle and boat-shaped; easy to remove.

Black Queen Cell Virus (BQCV).signs: Queen pupae turn black and die within sealed cell.
Black Queen Cell Virus (BQCV).symptoms: Failed queen rearing; often associated with Nosema.
Black Queen Cell Virus (BQCV).causes: Nosema infection acts as entry vector.
Black Queen Cell Virus (BQCV).myths: Chilled cells turn black (True, but BQCV is specific pathology).

Israeli Acute Paralysis Virus (IAPV).signs: Shivering wings; progression to paralysis and death.

Lake Sinai Virus (LSV).signs: Often asymptomatic; linked to weak colonies.
Lake Sinai Virus (LSV).myths: Newly discovered means new threat (Likely omnipresent but recently detected).

Slow Bee Paralysis Virus (SBPV).myths: Same as APV (False, different viral family).

Kashmir Bee Virus (KBV).symptoms: Highly virulent when injected by mites.

Small Hive Beetle.signs: Adult beetles fleeing light; clusters in corners.
Small Hive Beetle.symptoms: Fermented honey (slimed); 'rotten orange' smell; larva mining through comb.
Small Hive Beetle.causes: Weak colony unable to defend space; slimy honey harvest handling.
Small Hive Beetle.detection: Corrugated plastic traps; visual check of lid.
Small Hive Beetle.treatment: Swiffer sheets; Oil traps; Nematodes (Heterorhabditis indica) for soil.
Small Hive Beetle.prevention: Keep hives full of bees (no empty space); sunny location.
Small Hive Beetle.myths: beetles kill hives (False, beetle LARVAE kill hives).

Wax Moth (Greater & Lesser).signs: Silken tunnels (galleries) in comb; cocoons on frames.
Wax Moth (Greater & Lesser).symptoms: Destruction of brood comb; bald brood (uncapped pupae).
Wax Moth (Greater & Lesser).prevention: Strong colonies; Para-dichlorobenzene (PDB) for STORAGE ONLY.
Wax Moth (Greater & Lesser).myths: Moths kill colonies (False, they carry out the dead/weak).

Tracheal Mite.symptoms: Inability to cluster in winter; suffocation.
Tracheal Mite.treatment: Menthol crystals; Formic acid; Grease patties.
Tracheal Mite.myths: It's gone (False, just managed by genetics).

Braula Coeca (Bee Louse).signs: Reddish-brown wingless fly on queen's thorax.
Braula Coeca (Bee Louse).symptoms: Steals food from queen (trophallaxis). Does not suck blood.
Braula Coeca (Bee Louse).myths: It's a mite (False, it's a fly).

Tropilaelaps Mite.symptoms: Similar to Varroa but more severe.
Tropilaelaps Mite.treatment: Cannot survive without brood >3 days. Brood break.
action_steps: Report immediately if found outside Asia

Dysentery.causes: High ash/moisture content in winter food (honeydew/uncured ivy honey); nosema; confinement.
Dysentery.treatment: Cleansing flight (warm weather); feed pure sugar syrup.
Dysentery.myths: It is a disease (False, it is a symptom).

Chilled Brood.signs: Dead larvae at hive entrance; black/grey larvae in cells.
Chilled Brood.causes: Sudden cold snap; beekeeper opening hive too long; too few bees to cover brood.

Pesticide Poisoning (Acute).signs: Carpet of dead bees with tongues out (proboscis extension) at entrance.
Pesticide Poisoning (Acute).treatment: Remove poisoned pollen; feed syrup; move hive.
Pesticide Poisoning (Acute).myths: Herbicides are safe (False, adjuvants kill bees).

Queen Failure (Drone Layer).signs: Bullet-shaped cappings (drone brood) in worker cells; spotty pattern.
Queen Failure (Drone Layer).causes: Queen ran out of sperm; poor mating.
Queen Failure (Drone Layer).myths: Bees will fix it (False, they will die out).

Laying Workers.signs: Multiple eggs per cell; eggs on side of cell wall.
Laying Workers.symptoms: Drone brood in worker cells; noisy roar.
Laying Workers.treatment: Shake out bees 100 yards away; combine with strong hive.
Laying Workers.myths: Just add a queen (False, they will kill her).

symptoms.name: Perforated Cappings
symptoms.desc: Small pinprick holes in brood cell cappings.

symptoms.name: Greasy Bees
symptoms.desc: Adult bees appearing shiny, black, and hairless.

symptoms.name: K-Wing
symptoms.desc: Wings held at uncoupled angles resembling letter K.

symptoms.name: Ropy Larvae
symptoms.desc: Larval remains stetch out >2cm like mucus.

symptoms.name: Scale
symptoms.desc: Hardened black crust adhered tightly to bottom of cell.

symptoms.name: Mummies
symptoms.desc: Hard white or grey fungal lumps on bottom board.

symptoms.name: Dysentery
symptoms.desc: Brown/yellow fecal streaking on hive face.

symptoms.name: Crawlers
symptoms.desc: Bees unable to fly, crawling on ground in front of hive.

symptoms.name: Spotty Brood
symptoms.desc: Inconsistent brood pattern with many missed cells.

symptoms.name: Shotgun Pattern
symptoms.desc: Scattered brood pattern indicating failing queen.

symptoms.name: Melted Larvae
symptoms.desc: Larvae looking like melted candle wax.

symptoms.name: Sour Smell
symptoms.desc: Vinegar-like or sour odor from hive.

symptoms.name: Rotten Smell
symptoms.desc: Decaying meat or rotten orange smell.

symptoms.name: Absconding
symptoms.desc: Entire colony leaves the hive suddenly.

symptoms.name: Supercedure Cells
symptoms.desc: Queen cells built on face of comb.

symptoms.name: Swarm Cells
symptoms.desc: Queen cells built on bottom bars.

symptoms.name: Emergency Cells
symptoms.desc: Queen cells built from worker cells in center.

symptoms.name: Drone Layer
symptoms.desc: Bullet shaped cappings in worker cells.

symptoms.name: Multiple Eggs
symptoms.desc: Several eggs in one cell, often on walls.

symptoms.name: Small Bees
symptoms.desc: Smaller than average workers due to poor diet.

symptoms.name: Bleached Cappings
symptoms.desc: White cappings (fresh wax), sign of flow.

symptoms.name: Greasy Cappings
symptoms.desc: Contact with honey (dark look), valid variant.

symptoms.name: Phoretic Mites
symptoms.desc: Visible red mites on bee thorax/abdomen.

symptoms.name: Spinning
symptoms.desc: Bees spinning in circles on ground.

symptoms.name: Headless Bees
symptoms.desc: Typically hornets or wasps beheading bees.

symptoms.name: Washboarding
symptoms.desc: Bees rocking back and forth on front (cleaning).

symptoms.name: Quacking
symptoms.desc: Sound from virgin queen in cell.

symptoms.name: Pupal Tongue
symptoms.desc: Thin thread stretching from scale to roof.

symptoms.name: Hairless Bees
symptoms.desc: Bees look shiny and behave like robbers.

symptoms.name: Chilled brood
symptoms.desc: Dead brood on periphery of nest.

symptoms.name: Dead Pupae
symptoms.desc: Pupae chewed out with damaged eyes/legs.

symptoms.name: Chalky Pollen
symptoms.desc: Not to be confused with chalkbrood.

blog_posts.title: The Importance of Bees in Our Ecosystem
blog_posts.excerpt: Discover why bees are crucial for biodiversity and food production, and what we can do to protect them.
blog_posts.content_summary: Bees are keystone species essential for pollinating one-third of our food. Threats like habitat loss and pesticides are declining populations. We can help by planting bee-friendly gardens and supporting local beekeepers.

blog_posts.title: How to Identify Pure, Raw Honey
blog_posts.excerpt: Learn the key characteristics that distinguish authentic raw honey from processed alternatives.
blog_posts.content_summary: Tests for pure honey: Water Test (doesn't dissolve immediately), Texture (crystallizes over time), Burn Test (lights on match). Processed honey lacks pollen and enzymes found in raw honey.

blog_posts.title: Sustainable Beekeeping Practices
blog_posts.excerpt: Explore the methods we use to ensure healthy bee colonies and sustainable honey production.
blog_posts.content_summary: Sustainability involves respecting the hive (leaving honey for winter), natural disease management (IPM), and habitat preservation (diverse forage).

blog_posts.title: The Journey from Hive to Home
blog_posts.excerpt: Follow our transparent process from ethical harvesting to your kitchen table.
blog_posts.content_summary: Bees collect nectar, thicken it into honey. We ethically harvest cold-extracted honey, strain (not filter) it, and bottle immediately to preserve enzymes. Validated by HoneyChain.

blog_posts.title: Health Benefits of Raw Honey
blog_posts.excerpt: Understanding the nutritional and medicinal properties of unprocessed honey.
blog_posts.content_summary: Raw honey contains antioxidants, antibacterial/antifungal properties, and phytonutrients. It can heal wounds and support overall health.

blog_posts.title: Supporting Local Beekeepers
blog_posts.excerpt: How choosing ethical honey makes a difference for small-scale beekeeping communities.
blog_posts.content_summary: Buying local supports the economy, preserves traditional knowledge, and promotes better bee health by avoiding migratory stress.
